questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst runs a tightly controlled lab experiment with volunteers; what is likely high and what is at risk

options.text: Internal validity high, external validity at risk
External validity high, internal validity at risk

questions.explanation: Tight control boosts internal validity by reducing confounds, but artificial settings and volunteer samples can limit external validity. The trade-off is common in experimental research.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst uses an unreliable measure and small sample; which validity is threatened
questions.explanation: Statistical conclusion validity concerns whether statistical inferences are correct. Unreliable measures and small samples threaten it by inflating error or reducing power. It is distinct from causal or generalisability claims.
questions.hint: It is about statistical inference accuracy.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst loses many participants from the treatment group only; what threat arises
questions.explanation: Differential attrition can create group differences unrelated to treatment, threatening internal validity. Random attrition is less harmful but still reduces power. Track and report attrition.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst compares volunteers who chose training with non-volunteers; what threat is this
questions.explanation: Pre-existing differences between groups that self-select into conditions create selection effects, threatening internal validity. Random assignment prevents this. Volunteers often differ from non-volunteers.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst measures attitudes before and after a training that coincides with a major news event; what threat is this
questions.explanation: An external event occurring alongside the treatment can explain changes, creating a history effect. A control group measured at the same times helps isolate the treatment effect. Maturation and testing are different threats.
questions.hint: An outside event may explain change.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst measures children's skills over a year with no control group; improvement may reflect
questions.explanation: Natural development over time can produce improvement, a maturation effect. Without a control group, it is confounded with treatment. Control groups and shorter intervals help.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst gives a pretest then a posttest; score gains may partly reflect

options.text: Practice or familiarity from the pretest

questions.explanation: Taking a pretest can improve posttest performance through practice or familiarity, a testing effect. A control group with only posttest helps estimate this. It is distinct from maturation or history.
questions.hint: The pretest itself can boost scores.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst selects the lowest-scoring students for remedial training and sees improvement; what else could explain it
questions.explanation: Extreme scores tend to move toward the average on retest due to regression to the mean. Selecting low scorers makes improvement likely even without treatment. A control group helps distinguish.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst notices participants perform better when watched; what is this called

options.misconception: confuses observation with expectation of treatment

questions.explanation: Being observed can change behaviour, the Hawthorne or observer effect. Placebo involves expectations about treatment. Maturation and selection are different threats. Blinding and unobtrusive measures reduce observer effects.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst runs 20 t-tests on the same data; what problem arises
questions.explanation: Running many tests on the same data inflates the chance of at least one false positive, the family-wise error. Correction methods like Bonferroni control this. It is a multiple-testing problem.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst's 5 percent per-test alpha becomes a higher chance of any false positive across 10 tests; what is this called

options.misconception: confuses false positive with false negative

questions.explanation: The family-wise error rate is the probability of at least one false positive across a family of tests. It exceeds the per-test alpha. Power and effect size are separate concepts.
questions.hint: It is the chance of any false positive.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst runs 4 tests and wants family-wise alpha 0.05; Bonferroni per-test alpha is
questions.explanation: Bonferroni divides alpha by number of tests: 0.05/4 = 0.0125. It is conservative. Multiplying or using the wrong divisor gives incorrect thresholds.
questions.hint: Divide alpha by number of tests.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst reports an effect size of 0.8 in standard deviation units; what is this
questions.explanation: Cohen's d expresses the mean difference in standard deviation units, a standardised mean difference. It is not a p-value, correlation, or interval. It aids comparison across studies.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds r=0.5 between two variables; what is the shared variation
questions.explanation: Shared variation is r squared = 0.5^2 = 0.25 or 25 percent. r itself is not a proportion of variance. The remaining 75 percent is unshared.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants a narrower confidence interval; which factor helps most

options.misconception: changes confidence, not precision per se

questions.explanation: Larger sample size reduces standard error and narrows the interval while holding confidence constant. Lowering confidence also narrows it but changes the coverage. Effect size and variable count are not direct levers.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst has covariance 12, sd x=3, sd y=4; Pearson r
questions.explanation: r = covariance/(sd_x times sd_y) = 12/(3 times 4) = 1.0. This indicates a perfect positive linear relationship. Values must be within [-1,1].
questions.hint: Divide covariance by product of sds.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds event rate 0.20 in treated and 0.30 in control; risk difference
questions.explanation: Risk difference = 0.20 - 0.30 = -0.10. The negative sign indicates lower risk in the treated group. It is an absolute measure of effect.
questions.hint: Subtract control rate from treated rate.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst measures the same participants before and after training; which test is appropriate

options.misconception: confuses two time points with groups

questions.explanation: Paired (dependent) t-test is for the same subjects measured twice. Independent t-test ignores pairing and wastes power. Chi-square is for categorical data. ANOVA is for 3+ groups.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst tracks participants over 2 years with 20 percent dropout; what is retention
questions.explanation: Retention = 100 percent - 20 percent dropout = 80 percent. It measures how many remain. High retention reduces attrition bias. Report both retention and dropout.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference from a test statistic
questions.stem: An analyst has t=2.0 with n1=n2=25; approximate Cohen's d (t times sqrt(2/n) with n per group)
questions.explanation: d = t times sqrt(2/n) = 2.0 times sqrt(2/25) = 2.0 times 0.2828 = 0.566. This approximates Cohen's d for equal groups. It is a medium effect by conventional standards.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst reports p=0.03; what does this mean

options.text: There is a 3 percent chance the null is true
If null were true, data this extreme would occur 3 percent of the time

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability the null is true, nor effect size, nor practical importance. These are common misinterpretations.
questions.hint: It assumes the null is true.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst notes interval width depends on several factors; which increases width

options.text: All of the above decrease width

questions.explanation: Higher confidence requires a wider interval. Larger sample size and smaller standard deviation narrow it. The trade-off between confidence and precision is fundamental.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst reports p=0.001 but no effect size; why is this incomplete
questions.explanation: A small p-value can arise from a tiny effect in a large sample. Effect sizes convey magnitude, which p-values do not. Both are needed for interpretation. Effect sizes complement rather than replace p-values.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds a statistically significant 1 percent improvement in processing time; what is the concern

options.text: It must be a false positive

questions.explanation: Statistical significance says the effect is unlikely to be zero, not that it matters. A 1 percent gain may be too small to care about. Practical significance requires domain judgement. The result is still valid but possibly trivial.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds r=0.6 between ice cream sales and drowning; what can be concluded
questions.explanation: Correlation indicates association, not causation. A third variable, like hot weather, may explain both. Causal claims require experimental or strong quasi-experimental designs.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds a correlation between shoe size and reading ability in children; what is the lurking variable
questions.explanation: Age affects both shoe size and reading ability, creating a spurious correlation. Controlling for age removes the association. Shoe colour is irrelevant. Denying confounding ignores the obvious common cause.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst uses observational data to claim a training causes higher productivity; what is the concern

options.text: Observational data cannot support strong causal claims
No concern if n is large

questions.explanation: Observational designs lack random assignment, so confounds may explain associations. Causal claims are weaker. Large n does not fix confounding. Correlation is necessary but not sufficient for causation.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst compares two existing classes without random assignment; what threat is present
questions.explanation: Without random assignment, groups may differ before treatment, confounding the comparison. This is a quasi-experimental threat. Randomisation or pretest measures help. Sample size is separate.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst must obtain before enrolling participants; what is required
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires providing adequate information so participants can decide voluntarily. A signature alone is insufficient. Withholding information or paying participants does not substitute for informed consent.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst plans a study with human participants; what should be obtained first

options.text: Approval from an ethics review board
No approval needed for low risk

questions.explanation: An ethics review board evaluates risks, consent, and protections before the study begins. Funding or publication agreements do not replace ethics review. Even low-risk studies often need review.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst uses deception in a study; what must follow data collection

options.text: Debriefing to explain and remove deception

questions.explanation: Debriefing informs participants about deception, explains the true purpose, and addresses any harm. It is an ethical requirement after deception. Publication and payment do not replace it.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst registers hypotheses and analysis plan before collecting data; what is this called
questions.explanation: Preregistration documents hypotheses and plans before data collection, reducing p-hacking and HARKing. Post-hoc and dredging occur after data. It increases transparency but does not guarantee validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst verifies that the treatment group actually experienced the intended condition; what is this called
questions.explanation: A manipulation check verifies the treatment was delivered and perceived as intended. It is not a confound, control, or randomisation. It supports internal validity of the manipulation.
questions.hint: It verifies the treatment worked as intended.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst excludes outliers only after seeing results; what risk does this create
questions.explanation: Excluding data after seeing results can be used to obtain significance, inflating false positives. Pre-specified exclusion rules reduce this risk. Justification after the fact is weaker.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst cites only studies supporting their hypothesis; what bias is this
questions.explanation: Citing only supportive studies creates confirmation or citation bias, distorting the evidence base. A balanced review includes contradictory findings. Honesty does not fix selectivity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst cites a source they have not read, relying on a secondary summary; what risk is this
questions.explanation: Citing unread sources risks misrepresentation and propagating errors. Secondary summaries can distort findings. Read primary sources when possible. Efficiency does not justify inaccuracy.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst debriefs participants but withholds that deception occurred; is this adequate

options.text: No, debriefing must disclose the deception

questions.explanation: Adequate debriefing must disclose the deception and its purpose. Withholding it leaves participants misinformed. Participant comfort or positive results do not replace disclosure. Debriefing is required, not optional.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst compares current results to a historical baseline; what threat is this
questions.explanation: Historical comparisons are vulnerable to history effects and selection differences over time. They are not equivalent to randomised controls. A concurrent control group is stronger.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Judge an effect against a threshold
questions.stem: An analyst's effect size is 0.15 with a threshold of 0.20 for meaningful change; what conclusion

options.text: The effect is below the meaningful threshold

questions.explanation: Comparing the effect size to the pre-specified threshold shows it falls short of meaningful change. Significance and sample size do not change the magnitude. Interpret against the threshold.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst considers using participant data beyond the agreed scope; what is the concern
questions.explanation: Using data beyond agreed scope breaches the consent agreement and participant trust. Anonymisation does not override consent limits. Efficiency does not justify ethical breach. Re-consent if scope changes.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst must choose between a controlled lab and a field study; explain the validity trade-off

answer.exemplar: A lab study maximises internal validity by controlling confounds but may reduce external validity due to artificial conditions. A field study improves generalisability but risks confounds. The choice depends on the research priority and question.

questions.explanation: The trade-off is between causal clarity and generalisability. Labs control confounds; fields reflect reality. Neither is always better. The research question should guide the choice.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to improve statistical conclusion validity; which action helps

options.text: Use reliable measures and adequate power

questions.explanation: Reliable measures reduce error and adequate power reduces false negatives, both supporting statistical conclusion validity. Adding confounds, reducing n, or ignoring error worsens it.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to reduce attrition; which strategy helps
questions.explanation: Maintaining contact and offering incentives improves retention. Ignoring or silently excluding dropouts hides bias. Eliminating follow-up ends the study. Report attrition transparently.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst compares self-selected groups; best way to reduce selection effects
questions.explanation: Random assignment eliminates systematic pre-treatment differences. Self-selection worsens selection bias. Larger samples and different measures do not address selection. Randomisation is the key.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to control history effects; which design helps

options.text: A concurrent control group measured at the same times

questions.explanation: A concurrent control group exposed to the same events allows comparison. Longer duration increases history risk. No control removes comparison. Population change does not control events.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to control maturation; which design helps

options.text: A control group of similar participants

questions.explanation: A control group of similar participants matures similarly, allowing comparison. No measurement ends the study. Longer intervals increase maturation. Self-selection worsens bias.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to estimate testing effects; which design helps
questions.explanation: The Solomon four-group design includes groups with and without pretests, allowing estimation of testing effects. Only pretests cannot separate them. No control removes comparison. Interval length alone does not isolate testing.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst selects extreme scorers; what design control helps

options.text: A control group of equally extreme scorers

questions.explanation: A control group with equally extreme scorers regresses similarly, allowing comparison. No retest ends measurement. Larger samples do not fix regression. Deleting scores biases data.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to reduce observer effects; which strategy helps

options.text: Use blinded raters or unobtrusive measures

questions.explanation: Blinded raters and unobtrusive measures reduce observer effects. Telling raters the hypothesis worsens bias. More observation increases the effect. Removing measurement ends the study.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst plans 6 pairwise comparisons; which approach controls family-wise error

options.text: Apply a Bonferroni or similar correction

questions.explanation: Bonferroni or similar corrections control family-wise error. Running all at 0.05 inflates it. Larger samples improve power but not error rate. Selective reporting is a form of p-hacking.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst runs 5 tests with family-wise alpha 0.05; Bonferroni per-test alpha
questions.explanation: 0.05/5 = 0.01. Bonferroni is conservative but simple. Other methods like Holm are less conservative. Report the method used.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst has raw p=0.02 across 4 tests; Bonferroni-adjusted p is
questions.explanation: Adjusted p = raw p times number of tests = 0.02 times 4 = 0.08. It no longer meets 0.05. Compare adjusted p to alpha, not raw p.
questions.hint: Multiply raw p by number of tests.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst reports d=0.2; by conventional benchmarks this is
questions.explanation: By Cohen's conventions, 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. These are rough guides, not universal. Context matters for interpretation.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds r=0.4 between two measures; shared variation as percent
questions.explanation: r squared = 0.4^2 = 0.16 = 16 percent. The remaining 84 percent is unshared. This is the proportion of variance explained.
questions.hint: Square r and convert to percent.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst has mean 50, se 2, z 1.96; upper bound of 95 percent CI
questions.explanation: Upper bound = 50 + 1.96 times 2 = 53.92. The lower bound would be 46.08. The width is 7.84. SE reflects sampling variability.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst computes r=0.85 between two tests; what does this indicate
questions.explanation: r=0.85 indicates a strong positive linear association. It does not imply causation. Weak or no relationship is inconsistent with 0.85. Strength labels are rough guides.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds risk difference -0.05; what does the negative sign indicate

options.text: Higher risk in the treated group
Lower risk in the treated group

questions.explanation: A negative risk difference means the treated group has lower risk. It is an absolute measure. Small does not mean zero. Relative measures like risk ratio differ.
questions.hint: Negative means lower risk in treated.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst's paired t-test shows mean difference 3 with p=0.04; what can be concluded
questions.explanation: A significant p-value indicates the mean change is unlikely to be zero. It does not imply large magnitude or causation. Effect size and design determine those. The result is statistically significant.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst reports 90 percent retention in a 1-year study; what does this suggest
questions.explanation: 90 percent retention means 10 percent dropout, indicating good follow-up. It does not guarantee absence of attrition bias. Results remain valid but bias is possible. Report reasons for dropout.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference from a test statistic
questions.stem: An analyst has t=3.0 with 50 per group; converting to Cohen's d gives approximately
questions.explanation: d = 3.0 times sqrt(2/50) = 3.0 times 0.2 = 0.60. This is a medium-to-large effect by conventions. t and d differ in units. Report both when possible.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
